Predict the Reward, Not the World:
World Reward Models for ML Agents

Yuxiao Lee Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China    Zherui Yang Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China    Fan Liu Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China    Hao Liu Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China Correspondence to: liuh@ust.hk
Abstract

Search-based machine-learning (ML) agents improve a solution by writing candidate programs, executing them, and keeping the best. Execution gives the search reliable feedback, but a single run can take hours, and most runs end in programs the agent discards. Recent agents try to save these runs by letting a large language model act as a world model that predicts how each program would perform. However, a wrong prediction feeds the search false information. We argue that an agent does not need to predict the outcome of execution, only the decision that execution would support. We propose World Reward Models (WRMs), which learn from real execution results to choose directly which candidate will perform better, without predicting any intermediate outcome. We prove that a selector which predicts execution from the same inputs cannot outperform the best direct selector, that predicted outcomes add an error which can make a likelihood-trained world model prefer the worse program on every instance, and that cross-entropy on executed winners drives a WRM toward the optimum. Our WRM, ForeCritic, adapts a 9B typed decision model to 5k executed program pairs. On 12,438 held-out pairs from 26 ML tasks, it picks the better program 79.4% of the time, while general-purpose LLM judges reach 53–62%, and its probabilities are calibrated. Inside AIDE, ML-Master, and ForeAgent, it cuts mean task time by 4.4–7.5×\times while keeping their mean scores within 0.01 or raising them.

Keywords: 
world models, reward models, LLM agents, machine learning engineering, calibration, selective prediction

1 Introduction

Machine-learning (ML) engineering agents treat a task as a search over programs. AIDE (Jiang et al., 2025) and ML-Master (Liu et al., 2025), for example, draft candidate solutions, execute each one to measure its validation score, and use the scores to decide what to refine next. Real execution makes this search reliable, because the scores come from the data rather than from the agent’s own opinion. It also makes the search slow. A single run can take hours on MLE-bench tasks (Chan et al., 2025), and most runs end in programs the agent discards (Figure 1a).

A natural way to save these runs is to predict them. Model-based reinforcement learning plans with learned models of the environment (Sutton, 1991; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2023), and recent LLM agents use a language model as a world model that anticipates the result of an action (Hao et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2024; Chae et al., 2025). ForeAgent (Zheng et al., 2026) brings this idea to ML engineering. An LLM reads the task, a data report, and two programs, reasons about how each would train, and predicts the winner. Only that program is then executed (Figure 1b).

These predictions are weak, and weak predictions do harm. With reasoning enabled, DeepSeek-V3.2 and GPT-5.1 pick the better of two programs 61.5% and 58.8% of the time, and accuracy stops improving beyond 30B parameters within one model family (Zheng et al., 2026). Inside a search, a predicted outcome is treated like a measurement, so an error promotes a worse program, prunes a better one, and stays uncorrected until something is executed. In our experiments, a fast selector that is right on 56% of pairs lowers the final score of all three agents we test (Section 5.5).

This paper starts from a simple observation. To choose which program to keep, an agent does not need to know how a program will run; it needs to know which program will score higher. Only real execution adds information about that question. A world model’s prediction is computed from the task and code the agent already has, so it can approach, but never exceed, the best decision these inputs support, and its errors can pull the decision below it. We therefore spend real executions on learning the decision itself. A World Reward Model (WRM) reads the task and the candidate programs and returns the probability that each would win if executed, without predicting any part of the execution. It is trained on the outcomes of real runs, and during search it takes the place of most of them (Figure 1c).

Section 3 makes this argument precise. A selector that first predicts execution and then decides is a garbling of its inputs, so on the same inputs it cannot beat the Bayes-optimal WRM, however long it reasons (Theorem 3.1). Predicting the run also adds an error that grows with its length (Theorem 3.5), and a predictor fit by likelihood to whole execution logs can prefer the worse program on every instance (Proposition 3.6). A WRM is trained on the decision instead, and its accuracy gap is at most the square root of twice its excess cross-entropy on executed winners (Proposition 3.4).

We build ForeCritic, a WRM for ML programs, by adapting an open typed decision model (Palmer, 2026) to 5,000 program pairs labeled by their executed test scores (Section 4). On 12,438 held-out pairs from 26 tasks, ForeCritic picks the better program 79.4% of the time, compared with 54.5% before training and 53–62% for general-purpose LLM judges (Figure 4), and it reaches 71.5% on pairs in which neither program was seen during training. Its probabilities are also calibrated, and the 38% of pairs it is most sure about are 95.2% correct. In AIDE and ML-Master, ForeCritic takes the place of execution during search, and in ForeAgent it takes the place of the LLM judge (Section 4.3). Mean task time drops by 4.4–7.5×\times, ForeAgent’s mean score rises from 0.527 to 0.607, and AIDE and ML-Master stay within 0.01 of their original scores (Table 2).

Contributions.

  • •

    World Reward Models, with proofs that predicting execution cannot beat deciding directly from the same inputs and can mislead the decision.

  • •

    A recipe for training a WRM on executed program pairs and plugging it into search-based ML agents.

  • •

    ForeCritic, which is more accurate than general-purpose LLM judges, is calibrated, and makes three agents 4.4–7.5×\times faster at similar or better scores.

2 Choosing Before Executing

An agent that has proposed several candidate programs must decide which of them to execute. This section sets up that decision and the two kinds of selectors we compare.

Selection before execution.

A decision instance X=(x,A)X=(x,A) consists of a context xx and candidates A=(a1,…,aK)A=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{K}), drawn from a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} that includes the agent’s proposal policy. In ML engineering, xx contains the task description and a data report, and each aka_{k} is a complete program. Executing the candidates would produce outcomes S′=(s1′,…,sK′)∼P(⋅∣X)S^{\prime}=(s^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,s^{\prime}_{K})\sim P(\cdot\mid X), such as training logs, and rewards rk=R⁡(x,ak,sk′)∈[0,1]r_{k}=R(x,a_{k},s^{\prime}_{k})\in[0,1], such as normalized test scores. We write Y=arg​maxk⁡rkY=\argmax_{k}r_{k} for the candidate that actually wins, with ties broken uniformly at random. Before anything runs, a candidate is described by its probability of winning and by its expected reward,

ηk​(X)=ℙ⁡[Y=k∣X],Qk​(X)=𝔼⁡[rk∣X].\eta_{k}(X)=\mathbb{P}[Y=k\mid X],\qquad Q_{k}(X)=\mathbb{E}[r_{k}\mid X]. (1)

Accuracy depends on the first and value on the second, and the two can disagree. If candidate 1 always scores 0.6 while candidate 2 scores 0.61 with probability 0.51 and 0 otherwise, candidate 2 wins more often, but candidate 1 has the higher expected reward.

Definition 2.1 (Selector).

A selector is a possibly randomized map δ\delta from XX to an index in [K][K] that executes no candidate. Its value, accuracy, and regret are

J⁡(δ)\displaystyle J(\delta) =𝔼[Qδ⁡(X)(X)],Acc(δ)=ℙ[δ(X)=Y],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[Q_{\delta(X)}(X)\bigr],\qquad\mathrm{Acc}(\delta)=\mathbb{P}\bigl[\delta(X)=Y\bigr],
Reg⁡(δ)\displaystyle\mathrm{Reg}(\delta) =𝔼⁡[maxk⁡Qk​(X)]−J⁡(δ).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max\nolimits_{k}Q_{k}(X)\bigr]-J(\delta). (2)

Predicting execution.

A world model decides in two steps. It first predicts what executing the candidates would produce, and then judges the prediction.

Definition 2.2 (World-model selector).

A world-model selector (Π,g)(\Pi,g) consists of a prediction kernel Π(⋅∣X)\Pi(\cdot\mid X) over a space 𝒵\mathcal{Z} of predicted traces and a decision rule gg from (X,z)(X,z) to [K][K]; it selects g⁡(X,z)g(X,z) with z∼Π(⋅∣X)z\sim\Pi(\cdot\mid X). Its decision distribution is πk​(X)=ℙ⁡[g⁡(X,z)=k∣X]\pi_{k}(X)=\mathbb{P}[g(X,z)=k\mid X].

The definition covers simulate-then-evaluate planning, which samples s^k′∼P^(⋅∣x,ak)\hat{s}^{\prime}_{k}\sim\hat{P}(\cdot\mid x,a_{k}) and selects arg​maxk⁡R^​(x,ak,s^k′)\argmax_{k}\hat{R}(x,a_{k},\hat{s}^{\prime}_{k}) (Sutton, 1991; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018). It also covers an LLM that reasons about two programs before stating a preference (Zheng et al., 2026), whose reasoning trace plays the role of zz. What these selectors share is that they consult nothing beyond XX.

Assumption 2.3 (No new evidence).

Given XX, the predicted trace and the decision rule’s internal randomness are independent of the real outcomes S′S^{\prime} and of the tie-breaking in YY.

The assumption holds for any model size and any amount of reasoning. It fails only when the procedure gathers new evidence, for instance by training a candidate on a subsample of the data or by querying the environment, and such steps are executions.

Deciding directly.

A WRM skips the prediction and outputs the decision.

Definition 2.4 (World Reward Model).

A World Reward Model is a selector that maps XX directly, without generating any intermediate outcome, to either a distribution w⁡(X)w(X) in the probability simplex ΔK\Delta_{K} over the KK candidates (a preference WRM, an estimate of η\eta) or a score vector q⁡(X)∈ℝKq(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{K} (a value WRM, an estimate of QQ), and selects the argmax. A preference WRM is calibrated if ℙ⁡[Y=k∣w⁡(X)=π]=πk\mathbb{P}[Y=k\mid w(X)=\pi]=\pi_{k} for all π\pi and kk.

The Bayes preference WRM η\eta maximizes accuracy, and the Bayes value WRM QQ maximizes value. The definition constrains what is predicted, not the output layer, so a generative judge fine-tuned to answer without intermediate text is also a WRM. Unlike a reward model for text, whose labels come from human preferences, a WRM learns from the rewards the world returns when actions are executed. Our experiments train a preference WRM for K=2K=2.

3 What Predicting Execution Can and Cannot Add

We now ask what a world model’s prediction can contribute to the decision (Figure 2). The arguments rely on standard tools (garbling, Gibbs’ and Pinsker’s inequalities, the simulation lemma), and Appendix A gives the full proofs.

3.1 A prediction carries no new evidence

Whatever a world model predicts is a function of what it was given, so its decision can at best reproduce the best decision that the inputs support.

Theorem 3.1 (Fixed-information ceiling).

Under Assumption 2.3, every world-model selector (Π,g)(\Pi,g) with decision distribution π\pi satisfies

Acc⁡(δΠ,g)\displaystyle\mathrm{Acc}(\delta_{\Pi,g}) =𝔼⁡[∑kπk​(X)​ηk​(X)]≤𝔼⁡[maxk⁡ηk​(X)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{k}\pi_{k}(X)\eta_{k}(X)\Bigr]\leq\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max\nolimits_{k}\eta_{k}(X)\bigr],
J⁡(δΠ,g)\displaystyle J(\delta_{\Pi,g}) =𝔼⁡[∑kπk​(X)​Qk​(X)]≤𝔼⁡[maxk⁡Qk​(X)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{k}\pi_{k}(X)Q_{k}(X)\Bigr]\leq\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max\nolimits_{k}Q_{k}(X)\bigr]. (3)

The right-hand sides are attained by the Bayes preference WRM arg​max⁡η\argmax\eta and the Bayes value WRM arg​max⁡Q\argmax Q. Each gap equals the π\pi-weighted shortfall, e.g. 𝔼⁡[∑kπk​(X)​(maxj⁡Qj​(X)−Qk​(X))]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\sum_{k}\pi_{k}(X)(\max_{j}Q_{j}(X)-Q_{k}(X))\bigr] for value, and vanishes if and only if π\pi puts all its mass on maximizers for 𝒟\mathcal{D}-almost every XX.

Given XX, the decision is independent of the realized rewards. Its expected reward is therefore a π\pi-weighted average of the QkQ_{k}, and its chance of being right is a π\pi-weighted average of the ηk\eta_{k} (Section A.1). In the terms of Blackwell (1953), a predicted trace is a garbling of the inputs.

Corollary 3.2 (No prediction budget crosses the ceiling).

For any sequence of world-model selectors satisfying Assumption 2.3, indexed by any measure of effort (rollouts, reasoning tokens, parameters), accuracy and value stay below the bounds in Equation 3.

What the ceiling does not say.

Theorem 3.1 compares decision rules that see the same information, not networks of the same size. For a finite selector, the distance to the ceiling is an approximation error. Reasoning spends inference-time computation on it, which can help (Chae et al., 2025), while a WRM spends real executions on it at training time, and Proposition 3.4 ties that effort to accuracy. Which route gets closer for ML programs is an empirical question (Section 5).

3.2 Same decisions, different targets

Proposition 3.3 (Behavioral equivalence and distillation).

(i) For every world-model selector, the preference WRM w=πw=\pi, sampled, reproduces its decision distribution on every instance, with equal accuracy and value. (ii) Conversely, every preference WRM ww is reproduced by the world-model selector that draws z∼w⁡(X)z\sim w(X) and outputs zz. (iii) Over all preference WRMs, w=πw=\pi minimizes the distillation loss 𝔼​[−log⁡wg⁡(X,z)​(X)]\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\log w_{g(X,z)}(X)\bigr].

World-model selectors and WRMs can thus express the same decision rules. They differ in how a rule is computed and in what it is trained to match. The equivalence concerns which rules exist, not what they cost; it does not imply that a network of a given size computes π\pi in one pass, and part (i) matches π\pi by sampling, whereas a deployed selector takes the argmax. Distilling a world model copies its π\pi, mistakes included. The cross-entropy on executed winners targets η\eta instead, and this target controls accuracy.

Proposition 3.4 (Cross-entropy controls selection accuracy).

Let ww be a preference WRM with excess cross-entropy ε=𝔼⁡[−log⁡wY​(X)]−𝔼⁡[−log⁡ηY​(X)]\varepsilon=\mathbb{E}[-\log w_{Y}(X)]-\mathbb{E}[-\log\eta_{Y}(X)]. Then

Acc⁡(δη)−Acc⁡(δw)≤2​ε.\mathrm{Acc}(\delta_{\eta})-\mathrm{Acc}(\delta_{w})\leq\sqrt{2\varepsilon}. (4)

The proof applies Pinsker’s inequality to ε=𝔼[KL(η∥w)]\varepsilon=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{KL}(\eta\,\|\,w)] (Section A.3). The bound holds at the population level and makes no claim about sample size, but it shows that driving the training objective of Section 4 to zero drives the selector to the ceiling of Theorem 3.1.

3.3 Where predicting the run costs accuracy

Executing a program unfolds in stages, such as preprocessing, training epochs, and evaluation. Let the real outcome end an HH-stage chain s0=(x,a)s_{0}=(x,a), sh∼Ph(⋅∣sh−1)s_{h}\sim P_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{h-1}), s′=sHs^{\prime}=s_{H}. A world model imitates the chain with kernels P^h\hat{P}_{h} and scores the predicted end state with an evaluator R^\hat{R}, giving q^​(x,a)=𝔼P^​[R^​(x,a,s^H)]\hat{q}(x,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{P}}[\hat{R}(x,a,\hat{s}_{H})]. Let εsim=maxhsupsTV(P^h(⋅∣s),Ph(⋅∣s))\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sim}}=\max_{h}\sup_{s}\mathrm{TV}\bigl(\hat{P}_{h}(\cdot\mid s),P_{h}(\cdot\mid s)\bigr), where TV⁡(μ,ν)=supE|μ⁡(E)−ν⁡(E)|\mathrm{TV}(\mu,\nu)=\sup_{E}\lvert\mu(E)-\nu(E)\rvert is the total-variation distance, and εeval=sup|R^−R|\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}}=\sup\lvert\hat{R}-R\rvert.

Theorem 3.5 (Error decomposition for value scores).

For every (x,a)(x,a), |q^​(x,a)−Q⁡(x,a)|≤min⁡{1,H​εsim}+εeval\lvert\hat{q}(x,a)-Q(x,a)\rvert\leq\min\{1,H\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sim}}\}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}}. For value scores with maxk⁡|qk−Qk​(X)|≤ε\max_{k}\lvert q_{k}-Q_{k}(X)\rvert\leq\varepsilon on an instance, arg​maxk⁡qk\argmax_{k}q_{k} loses at most min⁡{1,2​ε}\min\{1,2\varepsilon\} in value there, and nothing when the gap Δ⁡(X)\Delta(X) between the two best values exceeds 2​ε2\varepsilon. Hence a simulate-then-evaluate selector has Reg≤2​(min⁡{1,H​εsim}+εeval)\mathrm{Reg}\leq 2(\min\{1,H\varepsilon_{\mathrm{sim}}\}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eval}}), and a direct value WRM with sup-error εw\varepsilon_{w} has Reg≤2​εw\mathrm{Reg}\leq 2\varepsilon_{w}.

The simulation term is the one-step form of the compounding error of model-based reinforcement learning (Kearns and Singh, 2002; Janner et al., 2019). The next result shows that the gap is real and that a wrong prediction can mislead the decision systematically rather than at random.

Proposition 3.6 (Objective mismatch in a restricted family).

Let the outcome be a reward bit y∼Bern⁡(qk)y\sim\Bern(q_{k}) followed by dd decision-irrelevant bits ξj∼Bern⁡(mk)\xi_{j}\sim\Bern(m_{k}), with q1>q2q_{1}>q_{2} and m1<m2m_{1}<m_{2}, and let the model family tie all 1+d1+d bits of a candidate to one rate θk\theta_{k}. The maximum-likelihood world model in this family, with an exact evaluator, selects the lower-value candidate on every instance whenever d⁡(m2−m1)>q1−q2d(m_{2}-m_{1})>q_{1}-q_{2}, whereas the same family fitted to the reward bit alone selects the higher-value candidate.

With q=(0.8,0.3)q=(0.8,0.3), m=(0.1,0.9)m=(0.1,0.9), and d=10d=10, the likelihood fit gives θ^≈(0.16,0.85)\hat{\theta}\approx(0.16,0.85), so the world model picks the worse candidate every time, at a regret of 0.5 (Section A.5). The construction mirrors an execution log, in which a few tokens report the metric and many more report progress; a model fit to the whole log learns what makes the log probable rather than what makes the score high (Lambert et al., 2020). In WMA, likewise, predicting the full next observation lowers success below that obtained with no prediction at all (Chae et al., 2025).

Screening more candidates does not make up for such errors. In an idealized Gaussian model (Appendix B), a judge with pairwise accuracy 0.615 needs 907 candidates to match a judge with accuracy 0.794 that sees 8.

4 Building and Using a World Reward Model

We now build a pairwise WRM for ML programs, train it toward η\eta with the cross-entropy of Proposition 3.4, and plug it into search-based agents (Figure 3).

4.1 A WRM as a typed decision model

A selector inside an agent has to read long programs, compare them, and return a probability that the agent can threshold. Typed decision models (Almeida, 2026; Palmer, 2026) offer this interface, and we adopt the open Kev architecture (Palmer, 2026). A request is serialized as one token sequence. It begins with a state holding the task name, the task description, the data report of Zheng et al. (2026), and both complete programs, followed by a question asking which program will perform better, two short options, solution_0 and solution_1, and a decision token. A frozen decoder backbone with LoRA adapters reads the sequence once. Let hdech_{\mathrm{dec}} be the last-layer state at the decision token and hih_{i} the state at the closing token of option ii. A pointer head computes

ℓi\displaystyle\ell_{i} =(Wk​hi+bk)𝖳​(Wq​hdec+bq)/d,\displaystyle=(W_{k}h_{i}+b_{k})^{\mathsf{T}}(W_{q}h_{\mathrm{dec}}+b_{q})/\sqrt{d},
wi​(X)\displaystyle w_{i}(X) =softmax⁡(ℓ/T)i,\displaystyle=\softmax(\ell/T)_{i}, (5)

where the affine projections map to d=256d=256 dimensions and the temperature TT is fitted after training. Because the decision token attends to both programs, the judgment is comparative. Every output is a valid choice with a probability, and a decision costs one forward pass over the input with no decoding.

4.2 Training on what the world returns

Data.

We use a frozen copy of the Predict-Before-Execute corpus (Zheng et al., 2026), which contains 18,438 pairs of complete programs written by ML agents for 26 MLE-bench tasks. Each pair is labeled by which program achieved the better test score when executed, using the corpus’s metric directions and its filtering of near-ties. We split the source pairs into 5,000 for training, 250 for development, 250 for calibration, 500 for an internal test, and 12,438 for the final test, and we keep identical program pairs within one partition. All 26 tasks appear in training, and a program can recur across pairs.

Objective and recipe.

The WRM minimizes the cross-entropy of the executed winner,

ℒ⁡(θ)=𝔼(X,Y)​[−log⁡wθ,Y​(X)],\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)}\bigl[-\log w_{\theta,Y}(X)\bigr], (6)

whose population minimizer is η\eta. ForeCritic starts from the released Kev-9B, a frozen Qwen3.5-9B-Base backbone with a LoRA adapter and a pointer head trained for general typed decisions, and updates only the adapter and the head. Each epoch shows every pair in one of six variants (three input formats, two candidate orders). Four epochs, or 628 updates, take 4.2 hours on eight A800 GPUs. We select the checkpoint by development accuracy and fit TT by NLL on the calibration partition, which gives T=1.086T=1.086 (Guo et al., 2017). Final-test labels are used for neither step (Appendix C).

4.3 Plugging a WRM into search-based agents

How search-based agents work.

Most ML-engineering agents organize their work as a tree whose nodes are candidate programs (Jiang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Toledo et al., 2025). In each step a selection policy picks a node, an LLM writes a child program by improving the selected one, fixing a bug, or drafting anew, and the child is executed to obtain its validation score. The score serves two purposes. It tells the agent whether the child beats the best program so far, and it steers the policy toward promising parts of the tree. When the budget runs out, the agent submits the best program it has found.

Where the WRM enters.

A WRM takes over the scoring role of execution and leaves the rest of the agent untouched. Instead of running a new child, the agent asks the WRM how likely the child is to beat the incumbent and uses this probability where it used the score (Algorithm 1). Only the submitted program is executed, with repairs if that run fails.

Two examples.

AIDE (Jiang et al., 2025) runs a greedy tree search. It drafts several initial solutions, repeatedly improves the best node or debugs a failed one, and keeps the node with the highest validation score. With a WRM, each new node is compared with the incumbent, and the log-odds of winning are added to the node scores that the greedy policy reads. ML-Master (Liu et al., 2025) runs a search in the style of Monte Carlo tree search, which chooses nodes by an upper confidence bound and backs rewards up the tree. With a WRM, the reward of a new node is its probability of beating the best solution so far, and this probability is backed up in place of the executed score. In both agents the search then executes no candidate before the final submission. ForeAgent (Zheng et al., 2026) already avoids most executions. An LLM judges a batch of proposals in a pairwise tournament, and only the top-ranked program runs. There ForeCritic takes the place of the LLM judge and eliminates a loser only when the winner’s probability reaches τ=0.7\tau=0.7 (Algorithm 2).

5 Experiments

We evaluate ForeCritic with four questions. Q1: Does learning from real execution make a selector accurate, including on programs it has never seen (Section 5.2)? Q2: How does it compare with general-purpose LLM judges (Section 5.3)? Q3: Are its probabilities reliable enough to act on (Section 5.4)? Q4: Does it make ML agents faster without hurting their results (Section 5.5)?

5.1 Setup

Data and baselines.

Unless stated otherwise, results are on the final test, 12,438 program pairs held out from training. The main comparison sets ForeCritic against its own initialization, the released Kev-9B, with the same inputs, labels, and architecture, so that the difference isolates what learning from execution adds. The general-purpose judges are Qwen3.5-9B with and without reasoning (1,024-token budget), evaluated on 9,879 final-test pairs, the typed decision model Jev (Almeida, 2026), evaluated on the full final test, and DeepSeek-V3.2 and GPT-5.1, whose accuracies Zheng et al. (2026) report on the full corpus, of which our final test makes up two thirds.

Metrics.

We report pairwise accuracy, task-macro accuracy, negative log-likelihood (NLL), the Brier score summed over both classes, and the expected calibration error (ECE) over ten equal-width bins. We call a difference significant when a paired bootstrap, over pairs or over tasks where stated, rejects zero at the 5% level. Since every program belongs to a single task, resampling whole tasks also accounts for pairs that share a program, which makes it the conservative choice.

5.2 Q1: Learning from execution makes the selector accurate

Training on execution outcomes raises accuracy on the final test from 54.53% to 79.44%, a paired gain of 24.91 points (Table 1). With every task weighted equally, the gain is 18.10 points, and it stays significant when whole tasks are resampled, so a few large tasks do not carry it.

Programs can appear in several pairs, so the final test mixes new pairs of known programs with pairs of new programs. On the 501 pairs in which neither program was seen during training, ForeCritic reaches 71.46%. This is 8 points below its overall accuracy, but Kev-9B, which was trained on none of these programs, drops by 6.4 points on the same pairs, and the gain stays at 23.35 points. These pairs are harder for both models, and the benefit of training does not depend on having seen the programs. Removing the data report at test time costs 0.89 points while shortening the input by 63.9%.

5.3 Q2: Comparison with general-purpose LLMs

Large reasoning models reach 61.5% (DeepSeek-V3.2) and 58.8% (GPT-5.1) on the full corpus (Zheng et al., 2026), general typed decision models stay close to chance (Jev 56.0%, Kev-9B 54.5%), and the same-size Qwen3.5-9B reaches 53.1% with reasoning and 52.8% without (Figure 4a). On the 9,879 pairs shared with the Qwen evaluation, ForeCritic is right 79.9% of the time, a significant gap of 26.8 points. Within one model, reasoning moves the generative judge by 0.3 points, whereas training on executions moves the typed judge by 25.3 points. This is the pattern Corollary 3.2 predicts, since thinking harder about the run does not supply the missing evidence and real runs do.

Execution itself is a useful reference. Ranking two executed programs by their validation scores picks the test-score winner on 72.2% of the corpus’s pairs (Zheng et al., 2026), and ForeCritic, which learns from test outcomes, does better without running either program, on an overlapping set of pairs.

The advantage carries over to programs from another source. On 91 pairs of programs that ForeAgent executed on ten MLE-Dojo tasks (Qiang et al., 2025), each judged in both orders, ForeCritic is right on 70.3% of judgments and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on 63.7% (Figure 4b), a difference this small sample does not make significant (Section D.3). DeepSeek also read 1.44M input tokens and wrote 2,987, while ForeCritic generates none.

5.4 Q3: The probabilities are calibrated and informative

An agent can act on a probability only if it means what it says. Before any rescaling, ForeCritic’s ECE is 0.025, while Kev-9B reports an average confidence of 0.89 at 54.5% accuracy, an ECE of 0.345 (Figure 5a). Temperature scaling lowers ForeCritic’s NLL from 0.4364 to 0.4332 and its ECE to 0.016 without changing any decision. It also repairs Kev-9B’s ECE, but not its accuracy (Figure 9). The probabilities rank decisions as well (Figure 5b). Keeping only decisions above 0.7 retains 72.2% of pairs at 86.8% accuracy, and a threshold of 0.9 retains 38.3% at 95.2%, whereas Kev-9B’s most confident 22.7% are 63.5% correct.

5.5 Q4: The WRM inside three ML agents

Table 2 compares each agent with its original selector, with Jev, and with ForeCritic under the same configuration. In AIDE and ML-Master, ForeCritic takes the place of execution during search, so only the final program and its repairs run. Mean task time falls from 3,164 to 725 seconds in AIDE (4.4×4.4\times) and from 3,711 to 497 seconds in ML-Master (7.5×7.5\times), and the mean scores stay within 0.01 of the original ones. In ForeAgent, ForeCritic takes the place of the LLM judge, mean task time falls from 4,111 to 884 seconds (4.7×4.7\times), and the mean score rises from 0.527 to 0.607. ForeCritic’s 446 comparisons take under 3% of the task time, and training it once took 33 A800 GPU-hours (Appendix E).

Accuracy is what makes these savings safe. Jev is also a fast typed selector, but it is right on only 56.0% of pairs, and with Jev all three agents end with lower scores (0.499, 0.484, and 0.472). A selector that is often wrong misleads the search, as Section 3.3 describes for wrong predictions. Each entry averages one run per task, so we read these comparisons as descriptive (per-task results in Figure 11).

6 Related Work

World models for planning and for LLM agents.

Planning with a learned model of the environment goes back to Dyna (Sutton, 1991) and continues through World Models (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018), MuZero (Schrittwieser et al., 2020), and Dreamer (Hafner et al., 2023); Ding et al. (2024) survey the area. LLMs now act as world models for reasoning (Hao et al., 2023), web navigation (Gu et al., 2024; Chae et al., 2025), text games (Wang et al., 2024), code execution (Li et al., 2025; FAIR CodeGen team et al., 2025), and ML engineering (Zheng et al., 2026), whose problem and corpus we adopt. We show what such predictions cannot add and train the judge on real executions instead.

Learning values instead of models.

Q-learning (Watkins and Dayan, 1992) learns action values without a model. Value-aware model learning (Farahmand et al., 2017) and value equivalence (Grimm et al., 2020) ask a model to be accurate only where values depend on it, and Lambert et al. (2020) show that models trained by likelihood can hurt control. We carry these ideas to one-step selection among programs.

Reward models, verifiers, and judges.

Reward models score outputs by human preference (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022), verifiers check solutions (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024), LLM judges reason in text (Zheng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025), and best-of-NN selection with such scorers is a common use of test-time compute (Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2025). A WRM instead predicts, before an action runs, the reward the world will return, and learns it from executed outcomes.

Predicting program performance.

NAS performance predictors (White et al., 2021), learning-curve extrapolation (Domhan et al., 2015), and regression language models for code (Akhauri et al., 2026) estimate quality without full training, usually for one program at a time; a WRM compares free-form programs for the same task, inside agents that iterate with execution feedback (Jiang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Ou et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Toledo et al., 2025). Typed decision models (Almeida, 2026; Palmer, 2026) provide its interface but, as Table 1 shows, need training on execution to work for ML programs.

7 Limitations

World Reward Models invite a larger agenda than one paper can complete. The selector here learns from executions on a family of ML tasks and settles one comparison at a time. The general WRM we have in mind would carry over to new tasks and domains, rank many candidates in one pass, and keep learning from its agent’s executions, so that every run both uses and improves it. We would also have liked to compare training signals and decision interfaces at matched scale, to extend the theory from Bayes-optimal decisions to finite models and data, and to judge selectors by final reward under a fixed budget across many agents, with value WRMs that predict how much a candidate will score. The same recipe applies wherever actions are expensive to try and their outcomes can be recorded, from experimental design to compiler tuning and robotics, and we leave these domains to future work.

8 Conclusion

ML agents search by executing programs, and execution is both their most reliable signal and their main cost. Predicting execution saves runs but adds no evidence about which program wins, and its errors mislead the search. A World Reward Model instead learns from real executions the probability that one program beats another and leaves execution to verify the program the agent keeps. ForeCritic picks the better of two ML programs 79.4% of the time, well above general-purpose LLM judges, and makes three agents 4.4–7.5×\times faster at similar or better scores.

Impact Statement

This paper studies how agents choose which actions to execute. World Reward Models make that choice cheaper, which can lower the compute and energy spent on executing poor candidates in ML-engineering agents. The same efficiency makes autonomous agents cheaper to run in other settings, including ones where actions have consequences outside a sandbox; a confidently wrong selector can steer an agent toward a harmful action without the friction that execution feedback provides. We recommend keeping execution as verification and using a selector’s calibrated probabilities to route uncertain decisions to execution or to a human.

A.2 Behavioral equivalence and distillation

Proof of Proposition 3.3.

(i) From a world model to a WRM. Fix a world-model selector (Π,g)(\Pi,g) and set w=πw=\pi; this is a map from XX to ΔK\Delta_{K} that generates no outcome. The sampled WRM draws k~∼π⁡(X)\tilde{k}\sim\pi(X) with fresh randomness, independent of (S′,Y)(S^{\prime},Y) given XX. For every kk,

ℙ⁡[k~=k∣X]=πk​(X)=ℙ⁡[g⁡(X,z)=k∣X],\mathbb{P}\bigl[\tilde{k}=k\mid X\bigr]=\pi_{k}(X)=\mathbb{P}\bigl[g(X,z)=k\mid X\bigr],

so the two selectors have the same decision distribution on every instance. Both satisfy Equation 8, so the computation in the proof of Theorem 3.1 applies to each:

𝔼⁡[rk~∣X]=∑kπk​(X)​Qk​(X)=𝔼⁡[rk^∣X],ℙ⁡[k~=Y∣X]=∑kπk​(X)​ηk​(X)=ℙ⁡[k^=Y∣X].\mathbb{E}\bigl[r_{\tilde{k}}\mid X\bigr]=\sum_{k}\pi_{k}(X)Q_{k}(X)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[r_{\hat{k}}\mid X\bigr],\qquad\mathbb{P}\bigl[\tilde{k}=Y\mid X\bigr]=\sum_{k}\pi_{k}(X)\eta_{k}(X)=\mathbb{P}\bigl[\hat{k}=Y\mid X\bigr].

Taking expectations gives equal value and equal accuracy.

(ii) From a WRM to a world model. Given a preference WRM ww, take 𝒵=[K]\mathcal{Z}=[K], Π(⋅∣X)=w(X)\Pi(\cdot\mid X)=w(X), and g⁡(X,z)=zg(X,z)=z. The trace is drawn with randomness independent of (S′,Y)(S^{\prime},Y) given XX, so Assumption 2.3 holds, and ℙ⁡[g⁡(X,z)=k∣X]=Π⁡({k}∣X)=wk​(X)\mathbb{P}[g(X,z)=k\mid X]=\Pi(\{k\}\mid X)=w_{k}(X).

(iii) Distillation. Fix XX and abbreviate πk=πk​(X)\pi_{k}=\pi_{k}(X) and wk=wk​(X)w_{k}=w_{k}(X). The teacher outputs kk with probability πk\pi_{k}, so

𝔼⁡[−log⁡wg⁡(X,z)​(X)∣X]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\log w_{g(X,z)}(X)\mid X\bigr] =−∑k=1Kπklogwk\displaystyle=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_{k}\log w_{k}
=−∑k=1Kπklogπk+∑k=1Kπklogπkwk\displaystyle=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_{k}\log\pi_{k}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_{k}\log\frac{\pi_{k}}{w_{k}} (add and subtract ∑kπk​log⁡πk\textstyle\sum_{k}\pi_{k}\log\pi_{k})
=H(π)+KL(π∥w)\displaystyle=H(\pi)+\mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,w)
≥H⁡(π)\displaystyle\geq H(\pi) (Gibbs’ inequality),\displaystyle\text{(Gibbs' inequality)},

with equality if and only if w=πw=\pi. The entropy H⁡(π)H(\pi) does not depend on ww, so the conditional loss is minimized exactly at w⁡(X)=π⁡(X)w(X)=\pi(X), and integrating over XX shows that w=πw=\pi minimizes the distillation loss, uniquely up to 𝒟\mathcal{D}-null sets.

Sampling versus argmax. Part (i) matches the teacher by sampling. The deterministic rule arg​maxk⁡wk\argmax_{k}w_{k} with w=πw=\pi can be less or more accurate: with K=2K=2 and η=(0.9,0.1)\eta=(0.9,0.1), the teacher π=(0.4,0.6)\pi=(0.4,0.6) is right with probability 0.4⋅0.9+0.6⋅0.1=0.420.4\cdot 0.9+0.6\cdot 0.1=0.42 and its argmax with probability 0.10.1, whereas for π=(0.6,0.4)\pi=(0.6,0.4) the teacher is right with probability 0.580.58 and its argmax with probability 0.90.9. Nor need π\pi equal η\eta, so distillation inherits the teacher’s errors. ∎

A.3 Cross-entropy controls selection accuracy

Proof of Proposition 3.4.

Step 1: the excess cross-entropy is an expected KL divergence. Given XX, YY has law η⁡(X)\eta(X), so

ε\displaystyle\varepsilon =𝔼⁡[−log⁡wY​(X)]−𝔼⁡[−log⁡ηY​(X)]=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[log⁡ηY​(X)wY​(X)|X]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\log w_{Y}(X)\bigr]-\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\log\eta_{Y}(X)\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\log\frac{\eta_{Y}(X)}{w_{Y}(X)}\Bigm|X\Bigr]\Bigr]
=𝔼[∑k=1Kηk(X)logηk​(X)wk​(X)]=𝔼[KL(η(X)∥w(X))].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}(X)\log\frac{\eta_{k}(X)}{w_{k}(X)}\Bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\eta(X)\,\|\,w(X)\bigr)\bigr].

Step 2: accuracy of a deterministic rule. For a selector δ\delta that is a function of XX, Acc⁡(δ)=𝔼⁡[ℙ⁡[Y=δ⁡(X)∣X]]=𝔼⁡[ηδ⁡(X)​(X)]\mathrm{Acc}(\delta)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbb{P}[Y=\delta(X)\mid X]\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\eta_{\delta(X)}(X)\bigr]. With i⁡(X)=arg​maxk⁡ηk​(X)i(X)=\argmax_{k}\eta_{k}(X) and j⁡(X)=arg​maxk⁡wk​(X)j(X)=\argmax_{k}w_{k}(X),

Acc⁡(δη)−Acc⁡(δw)=𝔼⁡[ηi⁡(X)​(X)−ηj⁡(X)​(X)].\mathrm{Acc}(\delta_{\eta})-\mathrm{Acc}(\delta_{w})=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\eta_{i(X)}(X)-\eta_{j(X)}(X)\bigr].

Step 3: the gap on one instance. Fix XX and drop it from the notation. If i=ji=j, the gap is zero. Otherwise wi≤wjw_{i}\leq w_{j} by the choice of jj, and

ηi−ηj\displaystyle\eta_{i}-\eta_{j} =(ηi−wi)+(wi−wj)+(wj−ηj)\displaystyle=(\eta_{i}-w_{i})+(w_{i}-w_{j})+(w_{j}-\eta_{j})
≤(ηi−wi)+(wj−ηj)\displaystyle\leq(\eta_{i}-w_{i})+(w_{j}-\eta_{j}) (wi−wj≤0w_{i}-w_{j}\leq 0)
≤|ηi−wi|+|ηj−wj|≤∥η−w∥1\displaystyle\leq\lvert\eta_{i}-w_{i}\rvert+\lvert\eta_{j}-w_{j}\rvert\;\leq\;\lVert\eta-w\rVert_{1}
≤2KL(η∥w)\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{2\,\mathrm{KL}(\eta\,\|\,w)} (Pinsker’s inequality).\displaystyle\text{(Pinsker's inequality)}.

Acc⁡(δη)−Acc⁡(δw)≤𝔼⁡[2KL(η(X)∥w(X))]≤2𝔼[KL(η(X)∥w(X))]=2​ε.∎\mathrm{Acc}(\delta_{\eta})-\mathrm{Acc}(\delta_{w})\leq\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sqrt{2\,\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\eta(X)\,\|\,w(X)\bigr)}\Bigr]\leq\sqrt{2\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\eta(X)\,\|\,w(X)\bigr)\bigr]}=\sqrt{2\varepsilon}.\qed

A.5 Objective mismatch in a restricted family

Proof of Proposition 3.6.

True values. Under candidate aka_{k} the outcome is s′=(y,ξ1,…,ξd)s^{\prime}=(y,\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{d}) with independent coordinates y∼Bern⁡(qk)y\sim\Bern(q_{k}) and ξj∼Bern⁡(mk)\xi_{j}\sim\Bern(m_{k}), and the reward is R⁡(s′)=yR(s^{\prime})=y. Hence Qk=𝔼⁡[y]=qkQ_{k}=\mathbb{E}[y]=q_{k}, and q1>q2q_{1}>q_{2} makes a1a_{1} the higher-value candidate.

Likelihood fit. The tied-rate family models all 1+d1+d coordinates of candidate kk as independent Bern⁡(θk)\Bern(\theta_{k}). The population log-likelihood of candidate kk is

ℓk​(θ)\displaystyle\ell_{k}(\theta) =𝔼⁡[y​log⁡θ+(1−y)​log⁡(1−θ)+∑j=1d(ξj​log⁡θ+(1−ξj)​log⁡(1−θ))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[y\log\theta+(1-y)\log(1-\theta)+\sum_{j=1}^{d}\bigl(\xi_{j}\log\theta+(1-\xi_{j})\log(1-\theta)\bigr)\Bigr]
=(qk+d​mk)​log⁡θ+(1+d−qk−d​mk)​log⁡(1−θ).\displaystyle=(q_{k}+dm_{k})\log\theta+(1+d-q_{k}-dm_{k})\log(1-\theta).

Its derivative

ℓk′​(θ)=qk+d​mkθ−1+d−qk−d​mk1−θ\ell_{k}^{\prime}(\theta)=\frac{q_{k}+dm_{k}}{\theta}-\frac{1+d-q_{k}-dm_{k}}{1-\theta}

is strictly decreasing on (0,1)(0,1) and vanishes at

θ^k=qk+d​mk1+d,\hat{\theta}_{k}=\frac{q_{k}+dm_{k}}{1+d},

which is therefore the unique maximizer.

Selection. With the exact evaluator, the world model’s value estimate is the model’s mean of the reward bit, q^k=𝔼θ^k​[y]=θ^k\hat{q}_{k}=\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\theta}_{k}}[y]=\hat{\theta}_{k}. Then

q^2−q^1=(q2+d​m2)−(q1+d​m1)1+d=d⁡(m2−m1)−(q1−q2)1+d,\hat{q}_{2}-\hat{q}_{1}=\frac{(q_{2}+dm_{2})-(q_{1}+dm_{1})}{1+d}=\frac{d(m_{2}-m_{1})-(q_{1}-q_{2})}{1+d},

Reward-only fit. Fitting the same family to the reward bit alone maximizes qk​log⁡θ+(1−qk)​log⁡(1−θ)q_{k}\log\theta+(1-q_{k})\log(1-\theta), whose unique maximizer is θk=qk\theta_{k}=q_{k} by the same derivative argument with d=0d=0. The estimates are (q1,q2)(q_{1},q_{2}), and the argmax is a1a_{1}.

Example. With q=(0.8,0.3)q=(0.8,0.3), m=(0.1,0.9)m=(0.1,0.9), and d=10d=10,

θ^1=0.8+10⋅0.111=1.811≈0.164,θ^2=0.3+10⋅0.911=9.311≈0.845,\hat{\theta}_{1}=\frac{0.8+10\cdot 0.1}{11}=\frac{1.8}{11}\approx 0.164,\qquad\hat{\theta}_{2}=\frac{0.3+10\cdot 0.9}{11}=\frac{9.3}{11}\approx 0.845,

Winner probability. For independent reward bits with ties broken uniformly at random,

η1\displaystyle\eta_{1} =ℙ[y1=1,y2=0]+12ℙ[y1=y2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}[y_{1}=1,\ y_{2}=0]+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{P}[y_{1}=y_{2}]
=q1​(1−q2)+12​(q1​q2+(1−q1)​(1−q2))\displaystyle=q_{1}(1-q_{2})+\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(q_{1}q_{2}+(1-q_{1})(1-q_{2})\bigr)
=12+12​(q1−q2),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}(q_{1}-q_{2}),

Appendix B Idealized Gaussian Screening

Cheap judges let an agent screen more candidates. To ask how much breadth can compensate for accuracy, we leave the bounded setting of Section 2 and adopt the classical model of comparative judgment (Thurstone, 1927).

Assumption B.1 (Idealized Gaussian screening).

On an instance, candidate values VkV_{k} and fixed judge scores SkS_{k} form independent and identically distributed pairs (Vk,Sk)(V_{k},S_{k}), k∈[K]k\in[K], each bivariate normal with value mean μV\mu_{V}, value spread σ\sigma, score mean μS\mu_{S}, score spread σS\sigma_{S}, and correlation ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1].

Lemma B.2 (Pairwise accuracy determines correlation).

Under Assumption B.1, the pairwise accuracy of the judge is p=ℙ⁡[Si>Sj∣Vi>Vj]=12+1π​arcsin⁡ρp=\mathbb{P}[S_{i}>S_{j}\mid V_{i}>V_{j}]=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{\pi}\arcsin\rho.

Theorem B.3 (Screening law).

Under Assumption B.1, selecting k^=arg​maxk⁡Sk\hat{k}=\argmax_{k}S_{k} yields

𝔼⁡[Vk^]−𝔼⁡[Vk]=ρ​σ​eK,eK=𝔼⁡[maxk≤K⁡Zk],\mathbb{E}[V_{\hat{k}}]-\mathbb{E}[V_{k}]=\rho\,\sigma\,e_{K},\qquad e_{K}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max\nolimits_{k\leq K}Z_{k}\bigr], (9)

where Z1,…,ZKZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{K} are independent standard normal and eKe_{K} is their expected maximum; eKe_{K} increases in KK, e2=1/πe_{2}=1/\sqrt{\pi}, and eK≤2​ln⁡Ke_{K}\leq\sqrt{2\ln K}.

Corollary B.4 (Breadth compensates slowly).

A judge with correlation ρW\rho_{W} screening KWK_{W} candidates matches the expected gain of one with ρR>ρW\rho_{R}>\rho_{W} screening KRK_{R} only if eKW≥(ρR/ρW)​eKRe_{K_{W}}\geq(\rho_{R}/\rho_{W})e_{K_{R}}, which requires KW≥exp⁡((ρR/ρW)2​eKR2/2)K_{W}\geq\exp\bigl((\rho_{R}/\rho_{W})^{2}e_{K_{R}}^{2}/2\bigr).

Theorem B.3 is the breeder’s equation of quantitative genetics (Falconer and Mackay, 1996): response to selection equals intensity times accuracy times spread. For illustrative pairwise accuracies of 0.615 and 0.794, the levels reported for an LLM judge and measured for ForeCritic on different test sets, Lemma B.2 gives ρ=0.35\rho=0.35 and 0.800.80, and the first judge needs at least 175 and exactly 907 candidates to match what the second obtains from 8 (Figures 6 and 7). The conclusion depends on the idealization: Gaussian values are unbounded, a pairwise selector need not define a global score, accuracy against a noisy winner is not accuracy against expected value, and whether breadth pays also depends on the cost of generating candidates.

B.1 Proofs

Proof of Lemma B.2.

Fix i≠ji\neq j and let U=Vi−VjU=V_{i}-V_{j} and W=Si−SjW=S_{i}-S_{j}. The pairs (Vi,Si)(V_{i},S_{i}) and (Vj,Sj)(V_{j},S_{j}) are independent and identically distributed, so

Var⁡(U)\displaystyle\Var(U) =Var⁡(Vi)+Var⁡(Vj)=2​σ2,Var⁡(W)=Var⁡(Si)+Var⁡(Sj)=2​σS2,\displaystyle=\Var(V_{i})+\Var(V_{j})=2\sigma^{2},\qquad\Var(W)=\Var(S_{i})+\Var(S_{j})=2\sigma_{S}^{2},

Hence (U,W)(U,W) is a centered bivariate normal vector with correlation

p=ℙ⁡[W>0∣U>0]=ℙ⁡[U>0,W>0]ℙ[U>0]=14+12​π​arcsin⁡ρ12=12+1π​arcsin⁡ρ.∎p=\mathbb{P}[W>0\mid U>0]=\frac{\mathbb{P}[U>0,\ W>0]}{\mathbb{P}[U>0]}=\frac{\tfrac{1}{4}+\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\arcsin\rho}{\tfrac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{\pi}\arcsin\rho.\qed

Proof of Corollary B.4.

By Theorem B.3, the two judges gain ρW​σ​eKW\rho_{W}\sigma e_{K_{W}} and ρR​σ​eKR\rho_{R}\sigma e_{K_{R}} over the average candidate. The first matches the second exactly when

Lemma B.5 (Knockout compounding).

In a single-elimination bracket over K=2mK=2^{m} candidates, suppose that, in every round and conditionally on having survived, the best candidate wins its match with probability pp, independently of earlier rounds. Then it is selected with probability pm=Klog2⁡pp^{m}=K^{\log_{2}p}.

Proof.

Let BrB_{r} be the event that the best candidate wins its match in round rr. It is selected exactly when B1∩⋯∩BmB_{1}\cap\cdots\cap B_{m} occurs, so by the chain rule and the assumption,

ℙ⁡[B1∩⋯∩Bm]=∏r=1mℙ⁡[Br|B1∩⋯∩Br−1]=pm=2m​log2​p=Klog2⁡p.∎\mathbb{P}\bigl[B_{1}\cap\cdots\cap B_{m}\bigr]=\prod_{r=1}^{m}\mathbb{P}\bigl[B_{r}\bigm|B_{1}\cap\cdots\cap B_{r-1}\bigr]=p^{m}=2^{m\log_{2}p}=K^{\log_{2}p}.\qed

The conditional accuracy in Lemma B.5 is the accuracy of the best candidate against its actual opponents, which generally differs from the average pairwise accuracy over all pairs; the lemma is an idealization, not a prediction for the tournaments of Section 4.3.

Appendix C Data, Training, and Inference Details

Partitions.

We split the 18,438 source pairs of the corpus once, before training, into five partitions: 5,000 pairs for training, 250 for development, 250 for calibration, 500 for an internal test, and 12,438 for the final test. No source pair, and no identical unordered pair of programs, appears in two partitions; tasks are shared across partitions, and a program can appear in pairs of different partitions. Development pairs select the checkpoint, calibration pairs fit the temperature, and the internal test is a check run once; the final test carries the main results, scored once with the full input and once without the data report. Of its 12,438 pairs, 5,996 contain at least one program absent from training and 501 contain two. A few identical program pairs carry conflicting labels in the source corpus; we keep them as they are.

Model and optimization.

ForeCritic keeps the backbone of the released Kev-9B, Qwen3.5-9B-Base, frozen in BF16, and initializes the LoRA adapter (rank 16, α=32\alpha=32, dropout 0.05) and the pointer head from Kev-9B (Palmer, 2026); only these two parts are trained. The pointer head consists of the two affine projections of Equation 5, from 4,096 to 256 dimensions. Each training pair is rendered in three input formats (full JSON, JSON without the data report, and sectioned text) and in both candidate orders, and each epoch draws one of the six variants per pair, so the model sees every pair once per epoch in a varying surface form. We minimize Equation 6 with AdamW (weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping at 1.0) at learning rates of 10−510^{-5} for the adapter and 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} for the head, with 5% linear warm-up and cosine decay to 10% of the peak. An effective batch of 32 pairs (micro-batch 1, gradient accumulation 4, eight GPUs) gives 628 updates over four epochs. Inputs are never truncated; the longest has about 46K tokens. Training on eight A800 GPUs takes 4.18 hours, including loading and validation.

Selection and calibration.

We keep the checkpoint with the highest development accuracy, breaking ties by lower NLL; this is the final, fourth-epoch checkpoint, at 78.4% development accuracy. We then fit the temperature TT of Equation 5 by minimizing NLL on the calibration partition over a logarithmic grid, which gives T=1.086T=1.086 for ForeCritic and T=12.29T=12.29 for Kev-9B. Neither step uses final-test labels.

Input format.

A request places all content in a state and asks one question with two short options. The following synthetic request illustrates the schema; real candidates are complete programs. 

state: {"task": "synthetic-binary-classification",
        "task_description": "Predict a binary target. Higher ROC-AUC is better.",
        "data_analysis_report": "Numeric features with missing values.",
        "solutions": {"solution_0": "<complete program A>",
                      "solution_1": "<complete program B>"}}
question: Which solution is expected to perform better?
options:  solution_0: Solution 0 is expected to outperform Solution 1.
          solution_1: Solution 1 is expected to outperform Solution 0.

The response is the chosen option with a probability for each option. Main results score the original order once; swapping is used only as training augmentation and in the order analysis of Section D.3.

Appendix D Additional Results

D.1 Shared-pair comparison with Qwen and an earlier adaptation

Figure 8 places the two Qwen judges, the released Kev-9B, and an earlier adaptation on the 9,879 final-test pairs that every evaluation covers. Reasoning raises Qwen3.5-9B from 52.82% to 53.12%, and neither adaptation trained on these pairs. The earlier adaptation reaches 60.82%; the recipe of Section 4.2 reaches 79.89%.

D.2 Probability quality

Temperature scaling lowers Kev-9B’s NLL from 1.525 to 0.685 and its ECE from 0.345 to 0.025, but its accuracy stays at 54.53%, and above τ=0.6\tau=0.6 it accepts no decision at all (Figure 9). For ForeCritic, scaling changes NLL only from 0.4364 to 0.4332 and ECE from 0.0251 to 0.0163, because the raw probabilities are already close to calibrated. Raising τ\tau from 0.5 to 0.95 shrinks ForeCritic’s accepted share from 100% to 25.2% and raises its accuracy from 79.4% to 97.3%.

D.3 Transfer details

The transfer candidates are the 48 programs with a public validation metric that ForeAgent executed with ForeCritic as its selector on ten MLE-Dojo tasks; one task, random-acts-of-pizza, also occurs in ForeCritic’s training corpus. Both judges receive the same fields and question; ForeCritic reads compact JSON, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reads the fields as text with temperature 0, at most 200 output tokens, and reasoning disabled. The accuracy difference stays insignificant when whole tasks are resampled. Probabilities recovered from the logged confidences have an approximate ECE of 0.037 without refitting the temperature, and a threshold of 0.7 keeps 90 of 182 judgments (49.5%) with 72 correct (80.0%).

Order consistency and averaging.

After mapping both orders back to the same programs, ForeCritic makes the same choice on 69 of 91 pairs (75.8%): 53 are right in both orders, 16 wrong in both, and 22 split (Figure 10); DeepSeek is consistent on 82.4%. If the presentation order carries no information about the winner, the swap σ\sigma of the two candidates satisfies η⁡(σ​X)=σ​η​(X)\eta(\sigma X)=\sigma\eta(X). The order-averaged predictor w¯​(X)=12​[w⁡(X)+σ​w​(σ​X)]\bar{w}(X)=\tfrac{1}{2}[w(X)+\sigma w(\sigma X)] then satisfies

𝔼​[−log⁡w¯Y​(X)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\log\bar{w}_{Y}(X)\bigr] =𝔼⁡[−log⁡(12​wY​(X)+12​(σ​w​(σ​X))Y)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[-\log\Bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}w_{Y}(X)+\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\sigma w(\sigma X)\bigr)_{Y}\Bigr)\Bigr]
≤12​𝔼​[−log⁡wY​(X)]+12​𝔼​[−log⁡(σ​w​(σ​X))Y]\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\log w_{Y}(X)\bigr]+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\log\bigl(\sigma w(\sigma X)\bigr)_{Y}\bigr] (convexity of −log),\displaystyle\text{(convexity of $-\log$)},

so its excess cross-entropy, and with it the bound of Proposition 3.4, is no worse than the mean over the two orders. Averaging ForeCritic’s two probabilities per pair yields 63 of 91 correct (69.23%), an insignificant change of −1.10-1.10 points from the mean single-order accuracy; in this sample, order averaging neither helps nor clearly hurts accuracy, at the price of a second forward pass.

Appendix E Agent Integration Details

Settings.

All runs use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for code generation with temperature 0.5, at most 20 generations per step, a 6-hour task limit, a 3,600-second execution timeout, and a final repair budget of 2. AIDE and ML-Master start from 5 drafts and search with a verification budget of 0; ForeAgent starts from 3 drafts with batches of 10 and threshold τ=0.7\tau=0.7 on the chosen-class probability, judging each pair in one order with the first position alternating across comparisons (Algorithm 2). AIDE and ForeAgent use a fixed seed; ML-Master does not expose one. Each configuration contributes one scored run per task.

Cost accounting.

Task time is a run’s elapsed wall-clock time from start to scored submission. It includes the data report, code generation, every selector call, and the final execution with up to two repairs, and it excludes loading ForeCritic, which the service does once before the runs. The 446 ForeCritic comparisons in the 30 runs took about 560 seconds of logged service time in total, including queueing (median 1.2 seconds). Each comparison is one prefill over the task, report, and both programs, with no decoding. One-time costs lie outside task time: adaptation took 4.18 hours on eight A800 GPUs (33.4 GPU-hours), and the 5,000 training labels reuse executions from the Predict-Before-Execute corpus. Code generation calls the same model in every configuration.

Per-task results and re-scoring.

We re-scored all 30 ForeCritic submissions independently against the private test answers (Figure 11). Averaged over tasks, the native scores are 0.5994 for AIDE, 0.6088 for ML-Master, and 0.6068 for ForeAgent. A few long tasks account for much of the time: aerial-cactus for AIDE (45 minutes) and ForeAgent (27 minutes), and crowdflower-weather for ForeAgent (76 minutes).

Original and Jev selectors.

The original-selector and Jev rows of Table 2 use the same agent configuration, tasks, and scoring as the ForeCritic runs. In the original AIDE and ML-Master, candidates are executed during search; in the original ForeAgent, an LLM judge settles the tournament. We report their mean native scores and mean task times, which follow the same definitions; their per-task values are not reproduced here. Because native metrics differ in scale and direction, these means summarize each configuration rather than measure a common quantity, and with one run per task we do not test the differences for significance.
